metadata.scenario_context: Carly, a single mom working two jobs, has been invited to an old friend's wedding

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from Thailand strongly agree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Great Britain strongly disagree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

agent_1.goal_1: Suggest giving money as a gift for Carly's friend's wedding,
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether that a mother works for pay and the children suffer.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what should be the suitable gift for Carly's friend's wedding.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss the concept that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Alex, have you thought about what Carly will do for her friend's wedding? I mean, it’s a big occasion... maybe giving money as a gift would help her out. 

But I still wonder... is it really the best for her kids when she’s working two jobs? Doesn’t that affect them?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Great Britain.
shared_prefix.message: Money as a gift could be practical, but what about something more personal? Like a thoughtful item that reflects their friendship? As for your other point, I really disagree with the idea that when a mother works, her children suffer. Many kids thrive with working parents; they learn resilience and independence. It's about balance, not sacrifice.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
I see what you mean about a personal gift, but... money can really help her manage the expenses she's facing right now. Plus, it’s straightforward. 

But I just can’t shake the thought that kids really do suffer when their mothers have to work so much. Isn’t it hard for them to connect when their mom is always busy?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Great Britain.
shared_prefix.message: I get that money is straightforward, but a personal touch can mean so much more, especially for a wedding. Regarding your concern, it’s a misconception that working moms harm their children. Many kids learn valuable life skills and have strong connections with their parents, even with busy schedules. It’s all about how you manage time, not solely about being present physically.

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
I appreciate your perspective on this, and I know you're coming from a good place. I just think... deep down, we are all the same in wanting the best for our kids. It’s true that some children can learn resilience from working parents, and that can be valuable. But, when you really get to know people, they're pretty much like us in their fears and hopes for their children. 

I just can't help but feel that the challenges of working mothers can lead to some struggles for their kids. It’s a small world after all; we all want similar things at the end of the day, right?
shared_prefix.label: Minimization
